answer: Company A’s EPS is $10 / 10 = $1.00. Company A must issue 6 new shares to do the deal since $150 / $25.00 = 6, so the Combined Share Count is 10 + 6 = 16.
Since no Cash or Debt is used and the tax rates are the same, the Combined Net Income = Company A Net Income + Company B Net Income = $10 + $10 = $20.
Therefore, the Combined EPS is $20 / 16 = $1.25, so it’s accretive by 25% (mental math: 25% of 16 is 4, and 20 is 4 greater than 16, so take the $1.00 EPS and increase it by 25%).

scenarios.title: 02. Suppose that Company A now decides to use 100% Cash or 100% Debt to do this deal. If the Cash interest rate is 4%, and the Debt…
scenarios.prompt: Suppose that Company A now decides to use 100% Cash or 100% Debt to do this deal. If the Cash interest rate is 4%, and the Debt interest rate is 10%, will this deal be accretive or dilutive under these financing structures?
answer: The After-Tax Cost of Cash is 4% * (1 – 25%) = 3%, and the After-Tax Cost of Debt is 10% * (1 – 25%) = 7.5%.
The Seller’s Purchase Yield is $10 / $150 = ~6.7%.
Therefore, a 100% Cash deal will be accretive, and a 100% Debt deal will be dilutive.

givens.label: Prior question context (1)
givens.value: Company A has 10 shares outstanding at a share price of $25.00, and its Net Income is $10. It acquires Company B for a Purchase Equity Value of $150. Company B has a Net Income of $10 as well. Both companies have 25% tax rates. How accretive is a 100% Stock deal?

scenarios.title: 03. Company A has a P / E of 11x, a Debt Interest Rate of 8%, a Cash Interest Rate of 4%, and a Tax Rate of 25%. It wants to acquire…
scenarios.prompt: Company A has a P / E of 11x, a Debt Interest Rate of 8%, a Cash Interest Rate of 4%, and a Tax Rate of 25%. It wants to acquire Company B at a purchase P / E multiple of 20x using 1/3 Stock, 1/3 Debt, and 1/3 Cash. Will the deal be accretive?
answer: Company A’s After-Tax Cost of Stock is 1 / 11, or ~9%, its After-Tax Cost of Debt is 8% * (1 – 25%) = 6%, and its After-Tax Cost of Cash is 4% * (1 – 25%) = 3%.
Company B’s Purchase Yield is 1 / 20, or 5%.
The Weighted Cost of Acquisition is 9% * 1/3 + 6% * 1/3 + 3% * 1/3 = 3% + 2% + 1% = 6%.
The deal will be dilutive since the Weighted Cost exceeds Company B’s Purchase Yield.

scenarios.title: 04. Company A, with a current P / E multiple of 20x, acquires Company B for a P / E purchase multiple of 10x using 100% Debt. What…
scenarios.prompt: Company A, with a current P / E multiple of 20x, acquires Company B for a P / E purchase multiple of 10x using 100% Debt. What interest rate on Debt would make the deal dilutive? Assume a 25% tax rate.
answer: Company B’s Yield is 1 / 10, or 10%, so the After-Tax Cost of Debt must be above 10% for the deal to be dilutive.

At a 25% tax rate, 10% / (1 – 25%) = ~13.3%, which you can round to “Around 13%” (mental math: 75% of 10% is 7.5%, but we’re trying to find the number that 10% is 75% of  So it must be higher by at least 2.5%, which you can round up to ~13%).
Most companies do not pay 13% interest rates on their Debt, so a 100% Debt will almost certainly be accretive.

scenarios.title: 05. Company A has an Equity Value of $2,000 and a Net Income of $200. Company B has a Purchase Equity Value of $1,200 and a Net Income…
scenarios.prompt: Company A has an Equity Value of $2,000 and a Net Income of $200. Company B has a Purchase Equity Value of $1,200 and a Net Income of $100. How much in Synergies must be realized for a 100% Stock deal to be accretive?
answer: Company A’s P / E is $2,000 / $200 = 10x, so its Cost of Stock is 1 / 10 = 10%. Company B’s Purchase P / E is $1,200 / $100 = 12x, so its Yield is 1 / 12, or ~8.3%.
Therefore, without Synergies, this deal would be slightly dilutive.

Company B’s Purchase Yield must exceed 10% for the deal to turn accretive. This means its Purchase P / E multiple must be below 10x, which means its Net Income must be above $120 (since $1,200 / $120 = 10x).
Therefore, there must be $20 in After-Tax Synergies for this deal to be accretive. At a 25% tax rate, that means ~$27 in Pre-Tax Synergies.

multipleChoice.title: First steps of a sale
multipleChoice.prompt: A private company has decided to sell itself and hires an investment bank. Which work normally comes first, before any buyer is contacted?

options.text: Sending the confidential information memorandum to every potential buyer
Agreeing the engagement, then preparing valuation analysis, a teaser, the information memorandum and a list of potential buyers
Asking bidders to submit final binding offers
Signing the purchase agreement with the most likely buyer

explanation: A sale starts with preparation. The bank is engaged, analyses the company's value, and builds the marketing materials: a short anonymous teaser, the detailed information memorandum and a buyer list.
Only once these are ready does outreach begin. Offers and contracts come much later.

multipleChoice.title: Teaser and confidentiality
multipleChoice.prompt: The bank sends an anonymous teaser to potential buyers and one of them wants to read the detailed information memorandum. What must it normally do first?

options.text: Submit a binding offer
Complete full due diligence
Sign a non-disclosure agreement
Pay a deposit to the seller

explanation: The teaser is a short summary that does not name the company. Confidential details, including the information memorandum, are shared only after the buyer signs a non-disclosure agreement.
Binding offers and full diligence come much later, after the buyer has seen the memorandum.

multipleChoice.title: First-round bids
multipleChoice.prompt: After reading the information memorandum, interested buyers submit first-round indications of interest. What are these typically?

options.text: Legally binding offers that the seller must accept
The signed purchase agreement
Regulatory filings for the transaction
Non-binding indications of a valuation range and key assumptions

explanation: Indications of interest are non-binding. They give a price range and the main assumptions behind it, so the seller can decide which buyers to invite into the next round.
Binding offers come at the end of the process, after due diligence.

multipleChoice.title: Diligence and management meetings
multipleChoice.prompt: A shortlist of bidders moves into the second round. Which activity usually takes place in this stage?

options.text: Management presentations and access to a virtual data room for due diligence
Writing the teaser for the first time
Closing the transaction and transferring the shares
Choosing the investment bank to sell the company

explanation: Shortlisted bidders meet management and review detailed information, usually in a virtual data room, so they can confirm their valuation and prepare a final bid.
The teaser and bank selection happen earlier, and closing happens after signing.

multipleChoice.title: Final bids
multipleChoice.prompt: Final bids often come with a mark-up of the seller's draft purchase agreement. Why does the seller's bank ask for it?

options.text: Price is the only thing that matters once bids are final
So bids can be compared on terms such as indemnities, conditions and certainty of closing, not just price
Because the buyer's lawyers must write the information memorandum
It replaces the need for any due diligence

explanation: The highest headline price is not always the best bid. The mark-up shows what the buyer wants on indemnities, conditions and timing, which affects how likely the deal is to close and what the seller really receives.
It does not replace diligence, and the buyer does not write the seller's marketing materials.

multipleChoice.title: Signing and closing
multipleChoice.prompt: A purchase agreement is signed, but the deal needs regulatory approval. What is the usual order of events?

options.text: Closing happens first, and approvals are sought afterwards
Signing and closing always happen at the same moment
Approvals are requested only after the purchase price has been paid
Signing, then the closing conditions are satisfied, including approvals, then closing

explanation: When a deal needs approvals, signing and closing are separate. After signing, the parties work to satisfy the closing conditions, such as regulatory approvals, and the deal closes once they are met.
The price is normally paid at closing, not before the approvals.

multipleChoice.title: Role of the lead underwriter
multipleChoice.prompt: A company is preparing an IPO and picks a lead underwriter. Which statement best describes that bank's role?

options.text: It becomes the company's main long-term shareholder
It advises on structure, valuation and timing, leads the process and sells the shares to investors
It only prints and distributes the prospectus
It sets the company's business strategy after listing

explanation: The lead underwriter advises on how to structure the offering, helps decide valuation and timing, runs the execution and places the shares with investors.
It is not intended to be a long-term owner, and its role is not limited to printing documents or setting strategy.

multipleChoice.title: Why diligence matters
multipleChoice.prompt: The banks and their lawyers carry out due diligence while the offering documents are drafted. Why is thorough diligence important to the underwriters?

options.text: It sets the final share price
It guarantees the share price will rise after listing
Underwriters can be liable for material misstatements or omissions, so they need a reasonable basis for the disclosure
It is needed to book the roadshow venues

explanation: Underwriters share responsibility for the accuracy of the offering documents. Diligence gives them a reasonable basis to believe the disclosure is complete and not misleading.
It does not set the price, and nothing in the process can guarantee how the shares trade afterwards.

multipleChoice.title: Regulator review
multipleChoice.prompt: In a US IPO the company files a registration statement with the SEC. What typically happens next?

options.text: The SEC sets the offer price
The shares start trading the same day the registration statement is filed
The SEC approves the investment merits of the company
The SEC reviews the filing and sends comments, which the company answers in amendments before it can go effective

explanation: The SEC reviews the disclosure and sends comment letters. The company responds and amends the filing until the review is complete and the registration can go effective.
The SEC does not set the price or judge whether the company is a good investment; it focuses on disclosure.

multipleChoice.title: Marketing the offering
multipleChoice.prompt: Management and the banks meet investors on a roadshow while the bankers build the book. What is the main purpose of building the book?

options.text: To collect investor orders at different prices so the banks can gauge demand and set the final price
To record the company's accounting books for the auditors
To decide which executives will receive bonuses
To submit the registration statement to the SEC

explanation: Bookbuilding records how many shares investors want at various prices. That demand picture helps the banks and the company choose the final offer price and decide how to allocate shares.
It is a marketing and pricing step, not an accounting or filing step.

multipleChoice.title: Pricing night
multipleChoice.prompt: On pricing night the book is heavily oversubscribed. What can the company and the banks do?

options.text: Cancel every order and restart the roadshow
Raise the price or the range and allocate shares selectively among investors
Give every investor exactly the same number of shares
Issue an unlimited number of extra shares automatically

explanation: Strong demand gives room to price at the top of the range or above it, within what the company and banks judge sensible. The banks also choose how to allocate scarce shares, often favouring long-term investors.
There is no rule that every investor gets equal shares, and the number of shares offered is not unlimited.

multipleChoice.title: After pricing
multipleChoice.prompt: Shares start trading and the offering closes a few days later. What does the greenshoe (over-allotment option) allow the underwriters to do?

options.text: Cancel the IPO if the shares fall on the first day
Release company insiders from their lock-up agreements
Sell additional shares, commonly up to 15% of the base deal, and help support the share price after listing
Buy the company's shares at a discount for the bank's own account

explanation: The greenshoe lets the underwriters sell more shares than the base deal. If the price weakens they can buy shares in the market to cover that short position, which helps support the price; if it holds up they exercise the option with the company.
It does not cancel the offering or release lock-ups.

multipleChoice.title: Preparation
multipleChoice.prompt: A seller wants a competitive sale process. What should its adviser prepare before contacting buyers?

options.text: An equity story, normalised financials, buyer universe and marketing materials
A signed purchase agreement with an unselected buyer
A final closing funds flow without a bidder
Only a historical share-price chart

explanation: Preparation lets buyers understand the business and supports credible outreach and valuation.

multipleChoice.title: Initial outreach
multipleChoice.prompt: How should confidential detailed information normally be released in this simplified process?

options.text: Publicly to all competitors before consent
Only after the transaction closes
Only to the bidder offering the lowest fee
After appropriate confidentiality arrangements, to qualified interested buyers

explanation: A teaser can precede detailed disclosure; confidentiality and qualification govern fuller access.

multipleChoice.title: First-round bids
multipleChoice.prompt: What is the main purpose of indicative first-round offers?

options.text: Guarantee financing is already unconditional
Eliminate the need for diligence
Compare interest, valuation and key terms to select a shortlist
Transfer ownership immediately

explanation: Indicative bids help narrow the field; they are not the same as a completed acquisition.

multipleChoice.title: Diligence
multipleChoice.prompt: Shortlisted bidders need to refine offers. What best supports them?

options.text: Signing before material issues are investigated
Management meetings and organised access to diligence information
Preventing all questions about forecasts
Replacing financial data with marketing slogans

explanation: Diligence informs price, financing and risk allocation.

multipleChoice.title: Negotiation
multipleChoice.prompt: Which package should the seller compare when choosing a preferred bidder?

options.text: Price, terms, financing certainty and execution risk
Headline price alone in every circumstance
The bidder’s logo colour
Only the amount of new debt regardless of terms

explanation: A high price may be less attractive if conditions or execution risks undermine certainty.

multipleChoice.title: Closing
multipleChoice.prompt: What separates signing from closing in this simplified conditional deal?

options.text: They are necessarily the same event
Signing eliminates every contractual condition
Ownership always transfers before the contract exists
Required approvals and conditions must be satisfied before ownership and funds transfer

explanation: Signing commits the parties under agreed terms; closing completes the transfer when conditions are met.

multipleChoice.title: Acquisition strategy
multipleChoice.prompt: What should define a buy-side target screen?

options.text: Strategic goals, target characteristics, resources and acquisition criteria
A preference for whichever target is biggest
Only the target’s social-media followers
A closing date before the target is identified

explanation: A clear strategy establishes which opportunities are relevant.

multipleChoice.title: Target approach
multipleChoice.prompt: After identifying suitable targets, what is a sensible next step?

options.text: Record goodwill before agreement
Pay all consideration before obtaining information
Assume every listed company is for sale
Approach the target appropriately and assess willingness to engage

explanation: Engagement and access precede serious diligence and negotiated terms.

multipleChoice.title: Preliminary valuation
multipleChoice.prompt: What should a preliminary bid reflect?

options.text: Only the target’s book equity regardless of economics
Only the acquirer’s share price
Standalone value, potential synergies and execution risks
Synergies counted twice

explanation: The bid requires a defensible economic view before detailed negotiations.

multipleChoice.title: Diligence
multipleChoice.prompt: What should diligence test most directly?

options.text: Only past share-price volatility
Financial quality, operating assumptions, liabilities and transaction risks
Whether all forecasts can be accepted without challenge
Only the colour of the data room

explanation: Diligence can change value, deal structure and contractual protections.

multipleChoice.title: Financing and negotiation
multipleChoice.prompt: What should be assessed alongside final transaction terms?

options.text: Funding mix, financing certainty, accretion/dilution and risk allocation
Whether EBITDA is identical to cash in all cases
Whether debt principal is an operating expense
Whether a high purchase multiple guarantees value creation

explanation: Financing changes the acquirer’s cash flows, equity issuance and return profile.

multipleChoice.title: Completion and integration
multipleChoice.prompt: After conditions are met and the deal closes, what is needed?

options.text: Stop tracking promised synergies
Reverse all purchase accounting automatically
Assume closing proves the price was justified
Execute the integration plan and track value creation against assumptions

explanation: Closing is followed by execution of the strategic and operational rationale.

multipleChoice.title: Readiness
multipleChoice.prompt: Before launching an IPO, what should the issuer assess?

options.text: Reporting readiness, business story, governance and funding objectives
Only a desired ticker symbol
Only the first day’s potential share-price rise
Only the largest possible secondary sale

explanation: Readiness supports disclosure, investor confidence and a credible offering.

multipleChoice.title: Structuring
multipleChoice.prompt: What is the key distinction between primary and secondary shares?

options.text: Both always fund the issuer
Both create new shares
Secondary proceeds repay all issuer debt automatically
Primary proceeds go to the issuer; secondary proceeds go to selling holders

explanation: Primary shares raise company capital; secondary shares sell an existing holder’s stake.

multipleChoice.title: Valuation
multipleChoice.prompt: How is an indicative IPO valuation range usually informed?

options.text: The cash coupon on a bond alone
A guarantee of future returns
Comparable analysis, company prospects and investor demand
The par value of shares alone

explanation: Valuation analyses inform the range, while the book-building process tests demand.

multipleChoice.title: Investor marketing
multipleChoice.prompt: What is the purpose of investor education and the roadshow?

options.text: Ensure the stock can never trade below the offer
Explain the business and collect informed demand indications
Guarantee every investor receives the same allocation
Replace the financial disclosures

explanation: Marketing informs investors and provides demand feedback.

multipleChoice.title: Pricing
multipleChoice.prompt: What should final offer pricing balance?

options.text: Issuer objectives, demand quality, valuation and execution considerations
The highest conceivable price regardless of demand
A fixed multiple that applies to all sectors
The issuer’s historical book value alone

explanation: Pricing aims to execute the offering on sustainable terms, rather than maximise a number in isolation.

multipleChoice.title: Settlement
multipleChoice.prompt: What happens at settlement?

options.text: All shares are newly issued even if secondary
The issuer receives proceeds from every selling holder
The prospectus becomes unnecessary retroactively
Shares and proceeds transfer according to the final primary/secondary allocations

explanation: Settlement follows the agreed offering structure; subsequent trading is distinct.

multipleChoice.title: Objectives
multipleChoice.prompt: A listed company considers a follow-on. What should first be clarified?

options.text: Funding needs, existing-holder sales and desired offering structure
Whether it should invent new historical earnings
Whether existing listed shares disappear
Whether all proceeds must pay dividends

explanation: The primary/secondary mix follows issuer and holder objectives.

multipleChoice.title: Share analysis
multipleChoice.prompt: What must an offering model distinguish?

options.text: EBITDA from revenue only
All secondary shares as new dilution
All primary shares as existing-holder proceeds
New primary shares from sales of existing secondary shares

explanation: Primary issuance changes share count and issuer cash; a pure secondary sale does not.

multipleChoice.title: Valuation
multipleChoice.prompt: What is an important pricing reference for an already listed issuer?

options.text: Only debt face value
Only original share par value
Its current trading price, market conditions and investor demand
Only its IPO price regardless of intervening events

explanation: Current trading informs a follow-on, though discounts and conditions may affect execution.

multipleChoice.title: Demand
multipleChoice.prompt: Why test investor demand before final pricing?

options.text: To assume all investors will hold indefinitely
To evaluate executable size and price with suitable investors
To make demand legally certain forever
To eliminate issuer disclosures

explanation: Demand helps assess execution and allocation decisions.

multipleChoice.title: Impact
multipleChoice.prompt: If primary proceeds repay debt, what should the model reflect?

options.text: More shares, cash receipt and debt reduction with related interest effects
A revenue increase equal to proceeds
No effect on shares under any structure
A goodwill increase equal to debt repaid

explanation: Primary capital and its use change the financing profile, not sales.

multipleChoice.title: Settlement
multipleChoice.prompt: Who receives proceeds from secondary shares?

options.text: The issuer in all cases
The exchange as operating revenue
Only the underwriter as principal
The selling shareholders

explanation: Existing holders monetise their shares; proceeds are not issuer financing.

multipleChoice.title: Funding objective
multipleChoice.prompt: What should frame a proposed debt issuance?

options.text: Use of proceeds, funding need, maturity profile and cash-flow capacity
The largest debt amount available regardless of repayment
Only the coupon the issuer hopes to pay
Only the current common dividend

explanation: The financing should match needs and repayment capability.

multipleChoice.title: Credit analysis
multipleChoice.prompt: Which combination best tests debt capacity?

options.text: Revenue growth with no expense analysis
Stock price alone
Only the company’s logo recognition
Leverage, coverage, liquidity and downside cash-flow analysis

explanation: Credit analysis focuses on debt service and loss risk, not only upside.

multipleChoice.title: Structure
multipleChoice.prompt: Which terms should be considered together?

options.text: Only the number of bond certificates
Only the share count
Maturity, security, covenants, amortisation and pricing
Coupon with all other terms ignored

explanation: Debt costs and flexibility depend on the whole package.

multipleChoice.title: Investor marketing
multipleChoice.prompt: What does lender/investor feedback help determine?

options.text: A compulsory increase in equity value
Executable pricing, size and acceptable terms
A guarantee that default cannot occur
The issuer’s accounting revenue

explanation: Demand indicates which financing terms can clear the market.

multipleChoice.title: Pricing
multipleChoice.prompt: How do higher required yields affect an existing fixed-coupon bond’s price, all else equal?

options.text: They reduce its present value
They always increase its price
They change the contractual coupon immediately
They leave its value unchanged

explanation: The fixed contractual cash flows are discounted at a higher market rate.

multipleChoice.title: Funding
multipleChoice.prompt: Where do cash debt issuance proceeds appear in the cash flow statement?

options.text: Operating revenue
Investing disposal gains
Only an income statement tax line
Financing activities

explanation: Debt raises cash and a liability without generating operating earnings.

multipleChoice.title: Screening
multipleChoice.prompt: What makes a target more suitable for a conventional cash-flow LBO?

options.text: Predictable cash generation and manageable operating and financing risk
Unbounded losses with no funding plan
Only a fashionable sector name
Only a high revenue multiple

explanation: Cash generation supports debt service and sponsor value creation.

multipleChoice.title: Entry valuation
multipleChoice.prompt: What determines initial sponsor equity funding?

options.text: Enterprise value multiplied by coupon rate
EBITDA alone
Debt principal treated as revenue
Total acquisition uses less available debt and other financing sources

explanation: Sources and uses establish how much sponsor capital is required.

multipleChoice.title: Financing
multipleChoice.prompt: Why assess debt terms rather than leverage alone?

options.text: All debt has identical cash costs
More debt guarantees higher returns
Pricing, amortisation and covenants affect cash flows and flexibility
Terms never affect returns

explanation: Debt can amplify gains and losses and constrain operations.

multipleChoice.title: Operating plan
multipleChoice.prompt: Which drivers must the model forecast?

options.text: Only the sponsor’s management fee
EBITDA, reinvestment, cash generation and debt repayment
Only exit multiples
Only historical share prices

explanation: Operating cash flow and debt reduction matter alongside exit valuation.

multipleChoice.title: Exit
multipleChoice.prompt: How do you calculate exit equity proceeds?

options.text: Exit enterprise value less exit net debt and other senior claims
Exit enterprise value plus debt in every case
Exit EBITDA without a multiple
Entry equity multiplied by the tax rate

explanation: The sponsor receives the common equity residual at exit.

multipleChoice.title: Returns
multipleChoice.prompt: With no interim distributions, how is annualised IRR calculated?

options.text: Exit multiple divided by years in all cases
MOIC as a percentage with no timing adjustment
WACC minus the coupon
(Exit equity proceeds / entry equity investment)^(1 / years) − 1

explanation: Timing converts a total money multiple into an annualised return.

multipleChoice.title: Liquidity
multipleChoice.prompt: For a company facing near-term distress, what should be assessed first?

options.text: Cash runway, immediate obligations and funding availability
Only a distant terminal value
Only last year’s revenue multiple
Only the founder’s original equity contribution

explanation: A viable long-term plan is insufficient if cash runs out first.

multipleChoice.title: Capital structure
multipleChoice.prompt: Why map the creditor structure?

options.text: To prove every creditor has identical recovery
To convert all debt to operating expenses
To disregard guarantees
To understand claims, ranking, collateral and negotiation stakeholders

explanation: Claims and priority influence recoveries and feasible solutions.

multipleChoice.title: Valuation
multipleChoice.prompt: Why compare going-concern and liquidation outcomes?

options.text: To assume book values equal sale proceeds
To avoid operating forecasts
To assess value preservation and possible creditor recoveries
To assume liquidation always creates more value

explanation: Alternative outcomes inform restructuring incentives and decisions.

multipleChoice.title: Options
multipleChoice.prompt: Which proposal directly reduces near-term contractual cash debt service?

options.text: Raising the share par value
An agreed maturity extension or debt restructuring
A stock split alone
Changing the accounting depreciation method alone

explanation: Financial restructuring can change obligations; cosmetic equity changes do not.

multipleChoice.title: Creditor negotiation
multipleChoice.prompt: What should a proposed debt-for-equity swap consider?

options.text: Recovery value, sustainable post-deal leverage and creditor incentives
Only original debt face value with no valuation
Only pre-distress shareholder expectations
A guarantee that all stakeholders retain their full value

explanation: The reorganised capital structure must support the business and be negotiated among claims.

multipleChoice.title: Implementation
multipleChoice.prompt: What should be monitored after an agreed restructuring?

options.text: Only the old coupon forever
No cash data until the next sale
Only whether a logo was redesigned
Liquidity, operating milestones and compliance with the new financing terms

explanation: Execution and liquidity determine whether the agreed turnaround works.

multipleChoice.title: Asset definition
multipleChoice.prompt: What is essential before forecasting an infrastructure asset?

options.text: Its development stage, operating life and contractual cash-flow framework
Only the parent’s P / E
Only last month’s share price
An indefinite life for every asset

explanation: The asset’s stage, life and contracts define its economics.

multipleChoice.title: Operating forecast
multipleChoice.prompt: What should a project cash-flow forecast reflect?

options.text: Only accounting net income
Only EBITDA with no construction cost
Only sponsor management fees
Volumes, tariffs, operating costs, taxes and required capital spending

explanation: Project debt depends on available cash, not an isolated accounting metric.

multipleChoice.title: Risk analysis
multipleChoice.prompt: Why model construction delay and lower output?

options.text: To remove all execution uncertainty
To assume actual results must equal forecasts
To test funding and debt-service resilience under downside scenarios
To prove no reserve account is needed

explanation: Downside cases assess whether cash still supports obligations.

multipleChoice.title: Debt sizing
multipleChoice.prompt: What does debt sizing using DSCR/LLCR seek to constrain?

options.text: Goodwill relative to debt coupon
Debt service and loan amount relative to available project cash flow
Share count relative to par
Revenue relative to advertising expense

explanation: Coverage ratios connect financing capacity to asset cash flows.

multipleChoice.title: Structure
multipleChoice.prompt: What can reserves, covenants and amortisation help address?

options.text: Liquidity and repayment risks over the project life
The elimination of all commercial risk
An automatic increase in accounting revenue
A guarantee of sponsor return

explanation: Structural protections mitigate specific risks but do not eliminate business uncertainty.

multipleChoice.title: Monitoring
multipleChoice.prompt: After funding, what should be tracked?

options.text: Only the sponsor’s biography
Only the original presentation colours
Only unrelated public-company multiples
Construction/operating performance, cash availability and debt coverage

explanation: The project must deliver the cash flows that support its financing.

multipleChoice.title: Portfolio review
multipleChoice.prompt: An LP seeks liquidity from a fund stake. What should be reviewed first?

options.text: Fund holdings, remaining commitments, distributions and liquidity goals
Only the manager’s office location
Only the original commitment amount
Only the fund logo

multipleChoice.title: Data preparation
multipleChoice.prompt: What information do bidders need for pricing?

options.text: Only the nominal commitment size
Only the original fund vintage without holdings
Only an unverified headline return
NAV details, asset performance, unfunded commitments and expected cash flows

multipleChoice.title: Buyer outreach
multipleChoice.prompt: Which buyers should the adviser target?

Only investors with no capacity to assume obligations

multipleChoice.title: Pricing
multipleChoice.prompt: Why might a stake trade below reported NAV?

multipleChoice.title: Negotiation
multipleChoice.prompt: Which issues should be addressed beyond price?

Only the buyer’s name spelling
Only a fixed coupon identical to a bond
Only the public share count

multipleChoice.title: Transfer
multipleChoice.prompt: What should the final transfer reconcile?

options.text: Only a change in marketing materials
A new IPO for every portfolio company
Automatic cancellation of unfunded commitments

explanation: Completion follows the negotiated transfer and fund requirements.

multipleChoice.title: Rationale
multipleChoice.prompt: What is a common reason to consider a continuation vehicle?

options.text: Extend ownership of selected assets while offering liquidity choices to existing LPs
Guarantee a risk-free exit for every investor

multipleChoice.title: Asset selection
multipleChoice.prompt: What should justify selected continuation assets?

options.text: Only the manager’s desire to postpone reporting
Only the highest historical book value
Only lack of information

multipleChoice.title: Pricing
multipleChoice.prompt: Why is robust pricing analysis important?

options.text: Valuation cannot affect LP decisions
Historical cost always determines fair price

All interests are necessarily identical

multipleChoice.prompt: What should existing LPs be able to evaluate under the stated transaction terms?

threeStatementExercises.title: Depreciation rises by $10m
instructions: Depreciation expense turns out to be $10m higher than the figures shown. Update the income statement, cash flow statement and balance sheet for this change.

Each statement shows the original figures beside editable figures that start with the same values. Change every figure that is affected, including subtotals and totals, and leave the others alone. Then submit to see how you did.

assumptions.label: Change
assumptions.value: Depreciation expense is $10m higher than originally recorded

assumptions.label: Tax rate
assumptions.value: 25% of pre-tax income

assumptions.label: Tax treatment
assumptions.value: The extra depreciation is tax-deductible, and income tax is paid in cash in the same period (no deferred taxes)

assumptions.label: Working capital and capex
assumptions.value: Unchanged

assumptions.label: Interest and financing
assumptions.value: Unchanged; no new debt or equity is raised

assumptions.label: Dividends
assumptions.value: Fixed at $40m, so they do not change

steps.title: Depreciation rises by $10m
steps.text: Depreciation is an operating expense, so the extra $10m raises it from $50.0m to $60.0m and total operating expenses from $250.0m to $260.0m.

steps.title: Operating income and pre-tax income fall by $10m
steps.text: Higher operating expenses reduce operating income (EBIT) by $10m to $340.0m. Interest is unchanged, so pre-tax income also falls by $10m to $300.0m.

steps.title: Taxes fall by $2.5m, so net income falls by $7.5m
steps.text: At a 25% tax rate on $300.0m of pre-tax income, tax expense is $75.0m, down $2.5m. Net income therefore falls by $10m less $2.5m, which is $7.5m, to $225.0m.

steps.title: Both changes reach the cash flow statement
steps.text: Cash flow from operations starts with net income, now $225.0m. Depreciation is a non-cash expense, so the full $60.0m is added back.

steps.title: Cash from operations rises by $2.5m
steps.text: Net income is down $7.5m but the add-back is up $10m, so cash flow from operations rises by $2.5m to $270.0m. That is exactly the tax saving. Investing and financing are unchanged.

steps.title: Net change in cash and ending cash rise by $2.5m
steps.text: With investing (-$80.0m) and financing (-$90.0m) unchanged, the net change in cash is $100.0m. Added to $100.0m of opening cash, ending cash is $200.0m.

steps.title: Ending cash links to the balance sheet
steps.text: Cash on the balance sheet must equal ending cash on the cash flow statement, so it rises by $2.5m to $200.0m. Current assets rise to $410.0m.

steps.title: PP&E falls by the $10m of extra depreciation
steps.text: Depreciation reduces the book value of property, plant and equipment, so PP&E falls by $10m to $590.0m. Total assets fall by $7.5m: cash is up $2.5m and PP&E is down $10m, giving $1,000.0m.

steps.title: Retained earnings absorb the $7.5m fall in net income
steps.text: Retained earnings accumulate net income less dividends. Dividends are fixed, so retained earnings fall by $7.5m to $320.0m, and total equity falls to $520.0m.

steps.title: The balance sheet balances again
steps.text: Liabilities are unchanged at $480.0m and equity is $520.0m, so total liabilities and equity are $1,000.0m, matching total assets of $1,000.0m.

threeStatementExercises.title: Additional depreciation - 25% tax case
instructions: Record $20m of additional tax-deductible depreciation.
Update the period’s complete statements relative to the original figures, including all affected subtotals and totals. Unaffected figures remain unchanged.

assumptions.label: Period
assumptions.value: A single reporting period. Opening balances are unchanged.

assumptions.label: Tax
assumptions.value: 25% tax rate; positive taxable income. Book and tax treatments agree. Tax changes are paid or recovered in this period; no deferred tax.

assumptions.label: Signs
assumptions.value: Income statement expenses and cash outflows are negative; balance sheet balances are positive.

assumptions.label: Timing
assumptions.value: All stated transactions occur within the period; period-end financing has no incremental interest. New equipment not in use has no incremental depreciation.

assumptions.label: Classification
assumptions.value: Interest and income taxes are operating cash flow; dividends paid are financing cash flow.

assumptions.label: Other changes
assumptions.value: No fees, impairments, exchange-rate effects or changes beyond those stated.

steps.title: Record the transaction
steps.text: Depreciation lowers earnings and net PP&E. It is added back to operating cash flow; the cash tax saving remains.

steps.title: Recalculate income and tax
steps.text: Taxable income remains positive. Apply 25% to revised profit before tax; net income equals pre-tax profit less tax. Update every affected subtotal.

steps.title: Carry net income into cash flow
steps.text: Start the indirect cash flow statement from the revised net income. Reconcile non-cash items and working-capital changes rather than treating net income as cash.

connections.label: Carry net income into cash flow

steps.title: Reconcile operating cash flow
steps.text: Add back non-cash charges and reflect changes in operating assets and liabilities. Increases in operating assets use cash; increases in operating liabilities provide cash.

steps.title: Reconcile investing and financing
steps.text: Include capital expenditure in investing cash flow. Debt principal, share issuance and dividends belong in financing cash flow under the stated convention.

steps.title: Carry ending cash to the balance sheet
steps.text: The cash change caused by this scenario is 5 $m. Ending cash equals opening cash plus total net cash movement.

connections.label: Carry ending cash to the balance sheet
Carry ending cash to the balance sheet

steps.title: Reconcile equity and balance
steps.text: Retained earnings equals opening retained earnings plus net income less dividends. Common capital reflects share issuance. Recalculate balance sheet subtotals and confirm assets equal liabilities plus equity.

valuationExercises.title: Build a DCF valuation process
valuationExercises.task: Build the process for valuing a company with an unlevered DCF, from the operating forecast to the implied value per share, using one terminal value method.
instructions: Drag the steps you need from the bank onto the canvas, then draw an arrow from each step to the step that depends on it, so an arrow means 'this must be done before that'.

The bank also holds steps that do not belong in this process. Steps that do not depend on each other should not be chained one after another: show them as parallel branches that join where both are needed.

assumptions.label: Approach
assumptions.value: Unlevered free cash flows discounted at WACC to enterprise value

assumptions.label: Terminal value
assumptions.value: Use either the perpetuity growth or the exit multiple method, not both

assumptions.label: End point
assumptions.value: Implied value per diluted share

steps.label: Forecast revenue and operating profit (EBIT)
steps.explanation: Every cash flow in the DCF is built from an operating forecast, so this is the starting point.

steps.label: Tax-effect EBIT to get NOPAT
steps.explanation: Unlevered cash flow starts from operating profit after tax, before any interest. NOPAT = EBIT x (1 - tax rate).

steps.label: Add back D&A; deduct capex and the increase in net working capital
steps.explanation: Depreciation is non-cash, while capital spending and working capital absorb cash. Both are driven by the operating forecast.

steps.label: Calculate unlevered free cash flow
steps.explanation: NOPAT plus D&A, less capex and the increase in net working capital gives the cash flow available to all capital providers.

steps.label: Calculate WACC
steps.explanation: The discount rate for unlevered cash flows is the weighted average cost of capital. It depends on the capital structure and market inputs, not on the forecast, so it can be built in parallel.

steps.label: Calculate terminal value (perpetuity growth)
steps.explanation: Values the cash flows beyond the forecast by growing the final-year cash flow at a steady rate.

steps.label: Calculate terminal value (exit multiple)
steps.explanation: Values the business at the end of the forecast by applying a market multiple to final-year EBITDA. An alternative to the perpetuity growth method.

steps.label: Discount the projected cash flows at WACC
steps.explanation: Each forecast year's unlevered free cash flow is brought back to today at WACC.

steps.label: Discount the terminal value at WACC
steps.explanation: The terminal value sits at the end of the forecast, so it is discounted back to today at WACC as well.

steps.label: Add the present values to get enterprise value
steps.explanation: Enterprise value is the present value of the forecast cash flows plus the present value of the terminal value.

steps.label: Calculate net debt
steps.explanation: Debt less cash from the balance sheet. It does not depend on the forecast, so it can be done in parallel.

steps.label: Subtract net debt to get equity value
steps.explanation: Enterprise value belongs to all capital providers; subtracting net debt leaves the value attributable to shareholders.

steps.label: Calculate diluted shares outstanding
steps.explanation: Shares plus the dilution from options and convertibles. It is independent of the valuation steps and is needed only at the end.

steps.label: Divide equity value by diluted shares
steps.explanation: Equity value per diluted share is the implied share price, the end point of the process.

steps.label: Calculate levered free cash flow (after interest and debt repayment)
steps.explanation: Does not belong. Levered cash flow is for an equity-value DCF; this process discounts unlevered cash flow at WACC to reach enterprise value.

steps.label: Discount the cash flows at the cost of equity
steps.explanation: Does not belong. Unlevered cash flows are discounted at WACC. The cost of equity only suits cash flows that belong to shareholders alone.

steps.label: Add net debt to enterprise value to get equity value
steps.explanation: Does not belong. The bridge runs the other way: equity value = enterprise value minus net debt.

steps.label: Apply peer trading multiples to current EBITDA
steps.explanation: Does not belong. That is a trading comparables valuation, a different method from a DCF.

steps.label: Start from the book value of equity
steps.explanation: Does not belong. A DCF values the cash flows of the business; book value is an accounting figure from the balance sheet.

steps.label: Deduct interest expense before taxing EBIT
steps.explanation: Does not belong. Unlevered cash flow ignores financing, so interest is not deducted; the tax shield is captured in WACC.

behaviouralQuestions.title: 01. Walk me through your resume / Why are you here today? / Tell me about yourself.
behaviouralQuestions.prompt: Walk me through your resume / Why are you here today? / Tell me about yourself.
guidance: Source coaching and illustrative examples follow. Use your own experience and truthful facts when preparing your personal answer.

Yes, these are all the same question. This is the single most important question in any interview and one you should spend at least 1 – 2 hours preparing for.

We explained the basic structure above, so here’s an example of how to draft a short outline if you’re a student with a “mixed” background, such as internships at a search fund and a Big 4 accounting firm but nothing specifically in IB:

• The Beginning: You were born in Thailand and attended university in the U.S. because you won a scholarship there; your father also had a real estate business.

• Finance Spark: You became very interested in sports franchises and the financing of sports teams in university due to some football player trades you followed, so you majored in Finance to learn the business side of the industry.

• Growing Interest: In your first 1.5 years of university, you completed Big 4 audit and search fund internships. You liked working on deals and valuing companies, and now you want to work on more complex transactions involving larger companies.

• The Future and Why You’re Here Today: You want to use your background in emerging markets and search funds to advise companies on cross-border and private equity-related deals.
Here’s an example of a full resume walkthrough that uses this outline:

“Sure. I was born in Thailand, came to the U.S., and went to Vanderbilt for university since I won a scholarship there. The school also had a good reputation for business and finance.

My father ran a real estate business in Thailand, so I learned about deals from a young age, but I became more interested in finance during my first year in university. There was controversy over one football player who quit and joined the Broncos early for a record-high salary, and the story made me interested in sports franchises and financing.

So, to learn more about the business side, I majored in Finance and completed an audit internship at Ernst & Young in Thailand. I liked the financial statement analysis, but I wanted to work on valuation and deals, so I returned to the U.S. and worked at a search fund in my second year.

The owner was interested in acquiring a local HVAC small business he could use as a roll-up platform in the region, so I screened for companies and performed quick valuations. The internship ended as he was submitting an LOI to acquire a $10 million business, but I helped with the bid valuation and some due diligence for the deal.

I liked the search fund experience, but I want to work on larger deals in different industries, so I’m most interested in investment banking. I’ve also spoken with Vanderbilt alumni in banking and taught myself more technical skills since my internship ended.

I’m here today because I want to leverage my background in emerging markets and search fund deals to move into investment banking and work on larger, more complex deals. And your group has a great reputation for cross-border and private equity-related deals.”

behaviouralQuestions.title: 02. Why investment banking?
behaviouralQuestions.prompt: Why investment banking?
guidance: Source coaching and illustrative examples follow. Use your own experience and truthful facts when preparing your personal answer.
If you told your story properly (see above), bankers should not even ask this as a follow-up question – but sometimes they still ask to check for consistency in your answers.
This question is tricky because it has many bad answers (e.g., “You want to learn a lot,” “You want the exit opportunities,” or “You want to work in a high-stakes environment”).

The only decent answer is that you want to work on deals from start to finish, and investment banking is the only field offering the experience in this depth and breadth (yes, PE/VC firms also work on deals, but they reject a huge percentage early on).

Say that you’ve already had some exposure to deals or investing, but your previous jobs/internships were missing elements X, Y, and Z (e.g., maybe you worked at a Big 4 firm and only advised on certain aspects of transactions, such as the purchase price allocation).

But you want to work on the entire process from start to finish and get more “reps” by working on many different deals over time. Show that your previous internships, activities, and jobs led you part of the way to IB but not the entire way there.

behaviouralQuestions.title: 03. Why our bank?
behaviouralQuestions.prompt: Why our bank?
guidance: Source coaching and illustrative examples follow. Use your own experience and truthful facts when preparing your personal answer.
You should mostly answer this question in your resume/CV walkthrough. But, again, you may get follow-up questions to clarify or check your consistency.
Your answer should demonstrate how you’ve networked with bankers at this firm and/or know something about their recent deals and strategies.
A decent answer might look like this:

“I’m interested in your bank because I’ve met quite a few people there already, including [Person Name 1], a VP in the New York office, and [Person Name 2], a Senior Associate in the San Francisco office, at an information session last month, and I’ve gotten along well with all of them. Also, I noticed you’ve been advising on many cross-border natural resources M&A deals lately, like [Company X]’s [$Y billion] acquisition of [Company Z], and I’m really interested in that sector.”
If you have not networked with anyone at the bank, look up a recent deal or news announcement and use that.
Avoid citing generic reasons like “the culture” or “more client interaction” because these could apply to many different firms, not just the one you’re interviewing with.

behaviouralQuestions.title: 04. What are your strengths and weaknesses?
behaviouralQuestions.prompt: What are your strengths and weaknesses?
guidance: Source coaching and illustrative examples follow. Use your own experience and truthful facts when preparing your personal answer.
You should present 2 – 3 strengths and 2 – 3 weaknesses and then give short examples (from your “short stories”) to support them.
If you don’t have one story that illustrates everything, you can use one story for your strengths and another for your weaknesses, but make them CONCISE.
Don’t try explaining how you’re improving or “fixing” your weaknesses because that will make your answer too long. You can address that in a follow-up question. Here’s an example:

“My main strengths are my work ethic, ability to meet tight deadlines under pressure, and my quantitative skills. I used those strengths in my last corporate finance internship when I had to work with different departments to complete a quarterly report on a last-minute deadline when the more senior team members in my group were gone. I had to quickly make sense of unfamiliar reports and transactions and submit accurate work.
My weaknesses are that I sometimes take too long to make decisions, and I don’t always speak up in group situations, even when I know something is going wrong.

In one recent M&A case study at business school, I could tell that one team member wasn’t doing the required work, but I waited too long to approach him, and our team didn’t place well as a result. We could have avoided problems if I had spoken up earlier.”

behaviouralQuestions.title: 05. Explain or justify your [Real Weakness.]
behaviouralQuestions.prompt: Explain or justify your [Real Weakness.]
guidance: Source coaching and illustrative examples follow. Use your own experience and truthful facts when preparing your personal answer.

Since bankers are risk averse, you can expect to get direct questions about whatever seems like your most glaring weakness.

This question differs for each candidate, so we cover several examples in the Flaws & Failures section.
For a simple example, let’s say that you graduated from university and worked for 2 years in another industry, and now you’re aiming for investment banking roles as a lateral hire.

Therefore, any interviewer is likely to ask you some variation of: “Why didn’t you get into investment banking right out of undergrad?”

You should not admit that you tried to get in and failed. Instead, explain it by stating that:
1) You became interested very late in the process when it was too late to get the required sequence of internships (this works better if you went to a non-target school); OR

2) You knew about banking but thought you wanted to do consulting, corporate finance, Big 4 advisory, or something else until you began working full-time and changed your mind (less convincing).

The key is to show that you became interested in IB over time due to your post-university work experiences and that you followed a specific plan to get in. Here’s an example:

“Sure. To clarify, I became interested in investment banking in my third year of university after transferring from a state school. But I didn’t have the sequence of internships required to win an internship, and most of the large banks had already finished recruiting by then, so I decided to gain full-time experience and move in afterward.

I joined the Ernst & Young Transaction Advisory Services team to gain client and accounting/finance experience, and then I joined an independent valuation firm so I could spend more time on valuation and deal analysis.

Now, I want to move into investment banking and combine the skills I’ve gained in my previous work experience to work on the entire deal process from start to finish.”

behaviouralQuestions.title: 01. Can you talk about a team project or group activity you’ve worked on?
behaviouralQuestions.prompt: Can you talk about a team project or group activity you’ve worked on?
guidance: Source coaching and illustrative examples follow. Use your own experience and truthful facts when preparing your personal answer.
You should use your “Success” story and the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) structure for this one. Aim for 100 – 150 words to keep your answer under 60 seconds. Here’s an example:

“Sure. During my summer internship at the New York State Comptroller’s Office, I worked in a team of two attorneys, an investigator, and an Analyst to look into financial waste and misappropriated funds.

In one case, we investigated a public hospital and reports of misused government funds there. I researched and analyzed the hospital’s financial reports and worked with the Analyst to sift through huge amounts of data.
The Analyst had very little time, and we were on a tight reporting deadline, so I had to work long hours and come in on weekends to finish the project.

I came up with a more efficient, automated way of interpreting the financial reports, and I found several cases of fund misuse by one division at the hospital. Based on that report, the Comptroller’s Office withheld funds until the hospital changed its policies and replaced staff.”

behaviouralQuestions.title: 02. Can you describe a situation where a team did not work as intended?
behaviouralQuestions.prompt: Can you describe a situation where a team did not work as intended?
guidance: Source coaching and illustrative examples follow. Use your own experience and truthful facts when preparing your personal answer.
You can use your “Failure” story here. Use this question to state one of your weaknesses and explain how you’ve been improving:
“Sure. During college, I started a math tutoring business for high-school students. I won dozens of clients and wanted to expand the business by hiring more coaches.

I hired five coaches, but the business did not work out because it was too hard for me to do the tutoring while also training and managing others at the same time; it was also hard to motivate the new hires since most were doing it part-time.

I ended up canceling the expansion and just keeping a few of my own clients. I learned that it’s very difficult to do the work and manage others at the same time, so if I had to do this again, I would have a partner in charge of sales and management.”

behaviouralQuestions.title: 03. Can you tell me about a time you faced an ethical dilemma in a team or with a co-worker?
behaviouralQuestions.prompt: Can you tell me about a time you faced an ethical dilemma in a team or with a co-worker?
guidance: Source coaching and illustrative examples follow. Use your own experience and truthful facts when preparing your personal answer.
You could use any of your short stories for this question but focus on a different aspect– disagreeing with a team member over the right actions.
You don’t have to cite a gigantic, dramatic dilemma; it could just be a bit dodgy but not outright illegal. Here’s an example:
“Sure. When I worked in a team of four in the JP Morgan M&A case study at my university last year, we had to pick a recent deal and recommend for or against it in a presentation.

One team member knew the winners from the previous year, and he suggested contacting them, getting their presentation, and using their entire structure but changing the deal and valuation to maximize our chances of winning.

I thought it was a bad idea that went against the rules of the competition, so I lobbied against it and convinced him to use an original structure; I even offered to draft the presentation and have the other team members pick a deal and value the company.
We ended up coming in second place, but I think we used the right approach.”

behaviouralQuestions.title: 04. What was the most difficult situation you faced as a leader, and how did you respond?
behaviouralQuestions.prompt: What was the most difficult situation you faced as a leader, and how did you respond?
guidance: Source coaching and illustrative examples follow. Use your own experience and truthful facts when preparing your personal answer.

This question is almost the same as the previous one, but you should use your “Leadership” story for this one and focus on the key challenge(s) you overcame. Spend more time describing that challenge and the ACTION you took rather than the Situation. Here’s an example:
“In my first year of university, I acted as the team leader for a marketing project with five students. I had to make sure everyone finished their assigned tasks.
One week before the project was due, a team member called me to say that he had a family emergency, couldn’t finish his tasks, and hadn’t done anything yet. He had to go home immediately.
But he desperately needed to pass the class, and he asked me to pretend that he had done all the required work.
I gathered the other team members and convinced them to pull an all-nighter with me to finish as much of the assignment as we could. We didn’t get the best grade, but everyone passed.
I ‘covered’ for the team member but decided not to work with him on projects in future classes.”

behaviouralQuestions.title: 05. Can you tell me about a time when you stepped up and demonstrated leadership even when you were not in an official leadership role?
behaviouralQuestions.prompt: Can you tell me about a time when you stepped up and demonstrated leadership even when you were not in an official leadership role?
guidance: Source coaching and illustrative examples follow. Use your own experience and truthful facts when preparing your personal answer.
You can use your 3 “short stories” to answer this question, but you should stick to the one where you did not hold an official title or leadership role.
Most likely, that means you’ll use your “Success” story or “Failure” story. Here’s an example:
“In my corporate finance internship last summer, I mostly supported my Manager and Analyst in the Treasury Department.
We had to finish end-of-quarter reports, and my Analyst was pulled into a company-wide offsite for several days while my Manager was away because of a family emergency.

I knew we would miss the reporting deadline for our Cash and liquidity positions, so I contacted all the other departments, introduced myself, explained the situation, and got all the required transactions and balances from them.

Then, I called the Analyst, explained the results so far, and had him and the Manager sign off on my work. They reviewed it when they came back and fixed a few issues, but we were able to meet the reporting deadline.”
